outline.chapter_title: Chapter 1: The Challenge of Aligning Large Language Models
outline.description: Introduces the fundamental problem of steering unsupervised language models towards specific human preferences. It contrasts the capabilities of raw pre-trained models with the need for behavioral control and outlines the limitations of current Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) pipelines.
subtopics: Capabilities and limitations of unsupervised pre-trained Language Models (LMs)
The necessity of aligning models with human values, safety, and specific tasks
Overview of the standard RLHF pipeline: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), Reward Modeling, and RL Optimization
Practical challenges of RLHF: instability, computational cost, complexity, and hyperparameter sensitivity
Motivation for a simpler, more direct approach to preference learning

outline.chapter_title: Chapter 2: Mathematical Foundations of Preference Learning
outline.description: Establishes the theoretical groundwork required to understand preference optimization. This chapter covers the statistical models used to represent human preferences and the mathematical formulation of the constrained reward maximization problem.
subtopics: The Bradley-Terry model for pairwise preferences
Formulating preference probabilities as a function of latent rewards
Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) for training explicit Reward Models
The Constrained RL Objective: Maximizing expected reward subject to KL-divergence constraints
The role of the Reference Policy ($\pi_{ref}$) in preventing mode collapse and ensuring stability

outline.description: The core technical chapter detailing the derivation of DPO. It explains how to mathematically map an optimal policy back to a reward function, allowing the elimination of the explicit reward model and RL loop in favor of a direct classification loss.
subtopics: Analytical solution for the optimal policy under KL-constrained reward maximization
Reparameterization technique: Expressing reward as a function of policy ratios ($r \propto \log(\pi/\pi_{ref})$)
Substituting reparameterized rewards into the Bradley-Terry model to cancel partition functions
Deriving the DPO Loss Function ($\mathcal{L}_{DPO}$): A binary cross-entropy objective over policies
Mechanistic interpretation: How DPO gradients adjust probabilities for preferred vs. dispreferred responses

outline.chapter_title: Chapter 4: Theoretical Properties and Stability Analysis
outline.description: Provides rigorous theoretical justification for why DPO works. It explores the equivalence between reward functions and policies, proves that DPO does not restrict the class of learnable rewards, and analyzes why traditional Actor-Critic methods suffer from instability compared to DPO.
subtopics: 'Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model': Equivalence relations between reward functions
_Lemma_: Identifiability issues in Plackett-Luce/Brunell-Terry models and how DPO resolves them via normalization
_Theorem_: Representational completeness—showing any valid reward class can be represented by a policy ratio
_Analysis_: Sources of instability in Actor-Critic algorithms (e.g., PPO) regarding value function estimation and baselines
_Comparison_: Why DPO's implicit normalization eliminates high-variance gradient updates
